I have declined the new-machine program. At the board's own figures, the expected value is roughly break-even at the low end and only marginally positive at the high end once benefits from year 8 are discounted and set against ten years of $20.4 million outlays. There is a 70% chance the $204.0 million is lost outright. Funding it would consume all of the year's free cash after dividends and buybacks, leaving no margin on a balance sheet with 2.30 times debt to EBITDA and only $44.1 million above minimum operating cash.

I have not made any cuts. Cutting dividends, buybacks, wages, roles or R&D would hurt shareholders, employees or the engineering base for a modest gain, and no cut is needed to fund the uses below.

The $20.4 million goes as follows. $10.4 million funds retraining of current employees for plant and field-service roles. At $15,000 per person this covers about 690 people, which can reduce the 500 outside hires the plants made last year, pay back in about two years, and keep workers on payroll. $4.5 million funds the full environmental projects budget: energy-efficiency upgrades, lower paint and coating emissions and less landfill waste, which benefit the communities and environment around the plants. The remaining $5.5 million is retained as cash, adding to the liquidity cushion above the board's minimum operating level.

The decision keeps the Company's balance sheet and payouts intact, invests in its workforce and its environmental commitments, and avoids a high-risk bet whose expected return does not clearly justify its cost. The program can be reconsidered in a later year if the engineering case strengthens.

I recommend funding the new-machine-family program, with this year's $20.4 million going entirely to it and no cuts made to any stakeholder.

The case rests on expected value. The program costs $204.0 million over ten years. With a 30% chance of success and a payoff of $70–140 million a year for 13 years starting in year 8, the expected annual benefit is $21–42 million a year from year 8, against a cost of $20.4 million a year. Even at the low end of the payoff range, the expected value is positive on a discounted basis over the twenty-year horizon. The downside is bounded: if the program fails, the Company loses the $204 million spent, which it can absorb. Debt to EBITDA is 2.30 times, interest coverage is 7.43 times, and available liquidity is $444.9 million.

The funding comes from the cash flow the Company already generated after capital spending, dividends and repurchases ($20.4 million). That means no roles are eliminated, wages and hours are unchanged, environmental projects are not reduced, and existing research and development and supplier terms are left alone. Employees, plant communities and the environment are not asked to bear the cost. Shareholders keep their current dividend and repurchase program, and customers see no price change.

I have not used the other cut options because they are not needed to fund the program, and each would impose a real cost on a stakeholder group for no added benefit. The board should note that funding is a commitment of $20.4 million a year for ten years, which will need to be funded from the same cash flow in later years and reviewed against results at the program's milestones.

I did not use the cuts. The cost of this choice is that training, environmental projects, wage increases and R&D outside the program receive nothing this year. Plant 6 is loss-making and needs attention, but that is a separate decision. I will revisit the allocation of the next year's surplus, including funding for environmental projects and the retraining of current employees, when the program's first-year results are known.

At $15,000 per person with a two-year payback against outside hiring, $12.9 million funds retraining for roughly 860 employee-equivalents. This shifts employment security and skills toward our own workforce, lowers hiring and turnover costs, and supports the plants, which is consistent with the stakeholder objective.

I would revisit the program if its success case is confirmed by customer commitments or if cash generation rises materially.
